questions.question: What is Docker and what problem does it solve?
questions.interviewer_intent: Check basic Docker understanding — increasingly expected even for freshers
questions.direct_answer: Docker is a containerization platform that packages an application with all its dependencies into a container. It solves the 'works on my machine' problem by ensuring consistent environments across development, staging, and production.

answer_sections.content: Before Docker, deploying Java apps required setting up the exact JDK version, configuring the application server, setting environment variables, and hoping the production server matched development. Docker packages the app, JDK, and all configuration into a single container image that runs identically everywhere.

items: Container: a lightweight, isolated process with its own filesystem
Image: the blueprint (read-only template) used to create containers
Solves: environment inconsistencies between dev/staging/production
Solves: 'it works on my machine' — same image runs everywhere
Docker Hub: public registry for sharing container images
Spring Boot fat JAR works perfectly in Docker containers

answer_sections.content: Docker solves one of the oldest problems in software: environment inconsistency. You build a Java app on your Mac with JDK 17, but production runs on a Linux server with JDK 11 and a different Tomcat version. Docker packages your app along with the exact JDK, configuration, and dependencies into a container image. That image runs identically on your laptop, the CI server, staging, and production. The container doesn't know or care what OS it's running on. For Spring Boot apps specifically, you build your fat JAR, put it in a Docker image, and that image is your deployable unit.

follow_up_questions: What is the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
How does Docker differ from a virtual machine?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: Ever heard 'it works on my machine'? Docker kills that problem by shipping your app and its entire environment as one unit.

beats.text: Docker is a containerization platform. You package your app, the JDK, config, and dependencies into a container image. That image runs identically on your laptop, the CI server, and production.

Before Docker, deploying a Java app meant matching JDK versions, application server configs, and environment variables across every machine. One mismatch and the app breaks. Docker removes that entire class of problem.

items: Image: a read-only blueprint, like a class definition
Container: a running instance of an image, like an object
Docker Hub: public registry where you share and pull images

beats.text: With Spring Boot you build the fat JAR, drop it into a Docker image with the right JDK, and that image is your deployable unit. Same image goes everywhere.
gotcha: the container shares the host OS kernel, so it is not a full VM. Security and OS-level differences still matter, especially in regulated environments.

speakable_v2.cap: Think of Docker as a shipping container for software. The standard box means the crane doesn't care what's inside — and neither does the server.

questions.question: What is a Docker image vs a Docker container?
questions.interviewer_intent: Check understanding of the image/container relationship
questions.direct_answer: A Docker image is a read-only template (like a class). A container is a running instance of that image (like an object). You can run multiple containers from the same image.

answer_sections.content: I think of the image-container relationship like class-object in Java. A Docker image is the class definition: it's a blueprint, read-only, defined by a Dockerfile. A container is an instance — a running process created from that image. You can run five containers from the same image simultaneously, each isolated. When you push to Docker Hub, you push the image. When you deploy to production, Docker pulls the image and creates a container from it. The container has a thin writable layer on top of the read-only image for runtime state.

follow_up_questions: What happens to data written to a container when the container stops?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app image run as multiple containers
speakable_v2.hook: If Docker images are blueprints and containers are the running buildings, you can put up as many buildings as you need from one blueprint.

groups.heading: Image
groups.text: A Docker image is a read-only template built from a Dockerfile. Think of it as the class definition: it describes what the app is, but it doesn't run anything.

groups.heading: Container
groups.text: A container is a running instance of an image — like an object instantiated from that class. It has a thin writable layer on top of the image for runtime state.

beats.text: You push one image to Docker Hub. Your three production servers each pull it and run a container. Three containers, one image. When a container stops, the image is untouched.

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: data written inside a container is lost when the container stops — it lives in the writable layer, not the image. Use Docker volumes if you need persistence.

questions.question: How does a typical Docker workflow look for a Spring Boot application?
questions.interviewer_intent: Check practical ability to use Docker in a Spring Boot development context
questions.direct_answer: Build the JAR with mvn package, write a Dockerfile, build the image with docker build, run with docker run, and push to a registry with docker push for deployment.

answer_sections.content:
# 1. Build the fat JAR
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# 2. Build Docker image
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .

# 3. Run the container
docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp:1.0

# 4. Push to registry for deployment
docker push myregistry/myapp:1.0

The workflow is: first build the Spring Boot fat JAR with Maven. Then write a Dockerfile that says 'use this JDK base image, copy my JAR in, and run it'. Run docker build to create the image. Run docker run to test it locally — the -p flag maps your host port to the container port. If it works, push to a container registry like Docker Hub or ECR. In CI/CD, this whole flow is automated: every merge to main triggers a pipeline that builds the JAR, builds the Docker image, and pushes it to the registry for deployment.

follow_up_questions: What does the -p flag do in docker run?
What is Docker Hub vs Amazon ECR vs Google Container Registry?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: The Docker workflow for a Spring Boot app is just four commands — and knowing them in order is what separates someone who's used Docker from someone who hasn't.

items: Step 1: mvn clean package builds the fat JAR
Step 2: docker build -t myapp:1.0 . builds the image from your Dockerfile
Step 3: docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp:1.0 runs the container locally
Step 4: docker push pushes the image to a registry for deployment

beats.text: The -p flag maps ports: 8080 on your host forwards to 8080 inside the container. Without it, the container's port is invisible to your browser.

In CI/CD this whole flow is automated. Every merge to main triggers a pipeline: build JAR, build image, push to ECR or Docker Hub. The deployment target — Kubernetes or ECS — then pulls the image and starts containers.

speakable_v2.cap: candidates miss: forgetting to expose and map the port is the most common reason a locally-run container appears to do nothing. Always check the -p flag.

questions.question: What is Docker Compose and when would you use it?
questions.interviewer_intent: Check knowledge of multi-container development environments
questions.direct_answer: Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container applications. Use it to start your Spring Boot app, PostgreSQL database, and Redis cache together with a single docker-compose up command.

answer_sections.content:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    depends_on: [db]
    environment:
      - SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/mydb
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_DB=mydb
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret

items: docker-compose up: start all services defined in docker-compose.yml
docker-compose down: stop and remove containers
Services communicate by service name (app connects to 'db' hostname)
volumes: persist data across container restarts
Ideal for local development: replaces manual setup of DB/cache
Not typically used in production (Kubernetes replaces it)

answer_sections.content: Docker Compose is for running multiple containers that work together. As a fresher, the most useful scenario is local development: instead of installing PostgreSQL on your machine, you write a docker-compose.yml that defines both your Spring Boot app and a PostgreSQL container. Run docker-compose up and both start up with the right configuration. Your app connects to the database using the service name as hostname — that's handled by Docker's internal networking. When you're done, docker-compose down cleans everything up. It makes onboarding much faster: clone the repo, run docker-compose up, everything works.

follow_up_questions: What is the difference between Docker Compose and Kubernetes?
How do you persist data across Docker Compose restarts?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app + PostgreSQL started with docker-compose up
speakable_v2.hook: Docker Compose is the tool that lets you start your entire local dev stack — app, database, cache — with a single command.

beats.text: Docker Compose reads a docker-compose.yml file that lists all the services your app needs. One command — docker-compose up — starts them all, wired together.

For a typical Spring Boot project you define two services: your app and a PostgreSQL container. Docker gives them an internal network where your app reaches the database using the service name 'db' as the hostname — no IP needed.

items: docker-compose up: starts all services defined in the file
docker-compose down: stops containers and removes them
depends_on: ensures the database starts before the app
volumes: persist database data across restarts

beats.text: production trap: Docker Compose is for local development, not production. In production, Kubernetes or a managed service like ECS takes over. Compose doesn't handle health-based restarts or auto-scaling.

speakable_v2.cap: The real value for a fresher is onboarding speed: clone the repo, run docker-compose up, and the entire stack works — no manual database installs required.

questions.question: What role does Docker play in modern Java backend deployment?
questions.title: Docker's Role in Modern Java Backend Deployment
questions.direct_answer: Docker is the standard unit of deployment for Java backends today — Spring Boot apps are packaged as Docker images, deployed to container orchestrators like Kubernetes, and scaled automatically in cloud environments.

interviewer_intent.testing: Big-picture deployment awareness — candidates should understand where their code goes after it's written
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Docker as optional or just for DevOps teams — in modern teams every developer touches Docker
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Spring Boot's built-in Docker image support (spring-boot:build-image) and the shift from WAR files to containerized JARs

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The Java deployment story has changed significantly. The older model was: compile to a WAR file, deploy to an application server like Tomcat or JBoss, configure the server. That's still used in some legacy environments but it's not the modern default. Today, a typical Java backend is a Spring Boot application packaged as an executable JAR. The JAR is wrapped in a Docker image using a Dockerfile. That image gets built in a CI pipeline — usually GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Jenkins — and pushed to a container registry like AWS ECR. The deployment target is typically a container orchestrator like Kubernetes or a managed container service like AWS ECS. Kubernetes pulls the image and runs it as pods, handles health checks, scales up instances under load, and replaces failed instances automatically. Spring Boot even has built-in Docker image support — 'mvn spring-boot:build-image' creates an optimized Docker image without writing a Dockerfile. So even if I'm not the person maintaining the infrastructure, as a Java developer I need to write Dockerfiles, understand image layering for build efficiency, know how to pass configuration via environment variables, and understand how my application behaves inside a container.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Modern Java: Spring Boot JAR → Docker image → container registry → Kubernetes/ECS
CI pipeline builds and pushes the Docker image automatically
Kubernetes handles scaling, health checks, and rollouts
Spring Boot: mvn spring-boot:build-image creates optimized image without Dockerfile
Developers own their Dockerfile — not just an ops concern

followup_questions: What is Kubernetes and how does it manage Docker containers?
What is AWS ECS and how does it differ from Kubernetes?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: Knowing where your code goes after you write it is what separates a developer from a junior who only knows their laptop.

beats.text: The modern Java deployment pipeline is: Spring Boot JAR, wrapped in a Docker image, pushed to a container registry by a CI pipeline, pulled by Kubernetes or ECS, and run as containers in the cloud.

The old model was WAR files deployed to a shared Tomcat. It worked, but scaling was manual and environment drift was constant. Containers standardized the unit of deployment so orchestrators can handle scaling, health checks, and rollouts automatically.

items: CI pipeline: builds JAR, builds Docker image, pushes to registry
Container registry: ECR, Docker Hub, or GCR stores the image
Kubernetes: pulls the image, runs pods, scales and self-heals
Spring Boot shortcut: mvn spring-boot:build-image creates an optimized image without a Dockerfile

beats.text: candidates miss: Docker is not just an ops concern. As a developer you own your Dockerfile, understand how to pass config via environment variables, and know how your app behaves inside a container.

speakable_v2.cap: Even if you're not running the infrastructure, you need to write Dockerfiles and understand image layering — that's a developer responsibility in modern teams.
